subject: identical values in main effect and interaction

messages.author: 24ddb890024f6d27
messages.subject: identical values in main effect and interaction
parts:
Hello!

I have two questions:

First, I would like to verify that ges (Generalized Eta Squared) is the so-called classic eta squared, rather than partial-eta-squared.

Second, my main question, is about a two-way mixed-effects ANOVA I did with ezANOVA. In the table of results (see below) I got identical values in the row of the between-subject effect and the row of the interaction.

$ANOVA
      Effect             DFn DFd         F            p                 p<.05        ges
2  Effect-Between     2  42       4.137886   2.289293e-02    *       0.08968521
3  Effect-Within        1  42    30.216347   2.094122e-06      *       0.26455361
4  Between:Within    2  42      4.137886   2.289293e-02      *       0.08968521

My question is if this could have happened accidentally or it is an indication of some statistical wrong-doing on my behalf or rather an expected by-product of certain designs.

Thanks!
dror

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] identical values in main effect and interaction
parts:
See the reference for generalized eta-squared in the help, but yes, it's more akin to classic eta-squared.

As for why you have the precise numbers you do, it's not clear but I agree it's suspicious. What does the output of ezStats give you (using all the same arguments as you put in the call to ezANOVA)?


--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: 265b547d9e4946a9
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] identical values in main effect and interaction
parts:
To add to Mike's response yes is sometimes closer (or identical) to classical and sometimes to partial eta squared depending on whether you have manipulated of measured factors and the type of design. The logic is that measured factors and covariates are part of the natural variability of what you are interested in. It therefore is misleading to ignore them (and individual difference) if you are trying to assess how much total variability is accounted for by an effect. Manipulated factors actually change the total variance so aren't part of the background 'natural' variability.

Partial eta squared is a horrible way to assess the practical effect size of an effect, because it doesn't use the total variability as a denominator. On the other hand it can be useful for planning power for a near-identical replication (same design, same factors etc.) because it ignore variability that doesn't impact on the error term.

Thom
